guard_streams.source: Automatic compensation: What you need to know
guard_streams.write_limit: Consumer compensation rules do not establish network availability, postcode coverage, or parcel-measured speed.

facts.detail: Ofcom lists the page as last updated on 20 July 2026.
The scheme page lists ten signed providers, with a stated TalkTalk network restriction.
Delayed-repair compensation starts when a stopped service is not fully fixed after two full working days.
The delayed-repair amount is £10.34 for each calendar day.
A missed appointment or cancellation with less than 24 hours notice carries £32.31 compensation.
Delayed start of a promised new service carries £6.46 for each calendar day of delay.
Simultaneous landline and broadband loss produces one compensation payment.
Compensation is normally credited no later than 30 calendar days after the relevant resolution or event.
For loss of service the customer reports the fault; payment becomes automatic after the repair threshold.
Exclusions include home equipment or activity, contract breach, and customer-caused or customer-prevented failure.

guard_streams.source: Making a complaint and using alternative dispute resolution schemes
guard_streams.write_limit: Complaint and dispute-resolution rules are service-process evidence, not parcel coverage or measured-speed evidence.

facts.detail: Ofcom lists the ADR guidance as last updated on 20 July 2026.
The customer should first contact the provider's customer-services department.
If initial contact does not resolve the issue, the customer should make a formal complaint.
Approved ADR is free to the customer and independently assesses unresolved complaints.
Eligibility includes residential users, small businesses up to ten employees and qualifying not-for-profits up to ten workers.
A complaint can proceed after six weeks or earlier with a deadlock letter.
Referral must be less than twelve months after receipt of a deadlock letter.
Providers must maintain an easily accessible complaints code of practice.
The code must include phone, postal and email or webform contact routes.
Ofcom currently approves CISAS and Communications Ombudsman.

guard_streams.write_limit: Switching-process guidance does not prove service availability at a postcode or parcel.

facts.detail: Ofcom lists the broadband-switching guide as last updated on 1 July 2026.
Under One Touch Switch the customer contacts the provider they want to move to.
The new provider arranges the broadband switch.
One Touch Switch provides information about applicable early-termination charges.
The customer supplies requested services, address and current-provider details.
When details match, the current provider sends information needed to decide whether to proceed.
The new provider arranges the preferred switch date where possible.
The old service ends automatically once the new service is working.
Provider-linked email may need migration or a continuation arrangement before switching.
The switching workflow is a consumer process and is not a network-coverage test.

guard_streams.source: Comparing customer service: choosing the best home broadband, mobile and landline provider
guard_streams.write_limit: Provider-level customer-service research cannot be written as parcel coverage, availability, or measured speed.

facts.detail: Ofcom lists the report page as last updated on 25 May 2026.
The page describes the publication as Ofcom's eighth comparative customer-service report.
The report covers residential telecoms customer experiences in 2024.
The 2024 results are compared with 2022 and/or 2023.
Ofcom moved to biennial reporting after the 2023 publication.
Overall satisfaction remained high across mobile, broadband and landline.
Satisfaction with complaints handling increased significantly in 2024 compared with 2022.
Call-abandonment rates vary considerably across providers.
The report records mixed results relating to broadband and landline faults.
EE resubmitted 2024 faults data in April 2026 and affected report figures were subject to restatement.

guard_streams.source: Broadband complaints fall to record low
guard_streams.write_limit: Complaint rates are provider-level service-quality indicators and do not establish physical coverage or measured speed.

facts.detail: Ofcom published the Q1 complaints update on 23 July 2026.
The latest figures cover January to March 2026.
Fixed-broadband complaints reached an all-time low of six per 100,000 customers.
The page compares Q1 2026 with a 2011 peak of 40 complaints per 100,000 customers.
Collective complaints decreased compared with Q4 2025.
TalkTalk generated the most fixed-broadband complaints in the latest figures.
Plusnet and Sky generated the fewest fixed-broadband complaints.
TalkTalk complaint themes included faults, service and provisioning, complaint handling, and billing, pricing and charges.
Ofcom states that it cannot act on individual complaints.
The metric compares providers using complaints per 100,000 customers.

guard_streams.source: Project Gigabit National Rolling Open Market Review May 2026
guard_streams.write_limit: Supplier-declared existing and planned build requires exact current-status and parcel-identity validation before any coverage promotion.

facts.detail: BDUK published the May 2026 National Rolling Open Market Review on 1 May 2026.
The consultation outcome records formal closure on 1 June 2026.
The consultation ran from 3pm on 1 May to 5pm on 1 June 2026.
The request invited suppliers to submit information about existing and planned build.
The request describes submissions at premises level.
The planned-build horizon covers the next three years.
The review covers the UK.
BDUK states that the rolling review takes place in January, May and September.
The source explicitly combines currently existing infrastructure with planned build, requiring semantic separation.
A planned-build record is not treated as current availability.

guard_streams.write_limit: Market-level and consumer-research data cannot establish exact postcode or parcel availability without an approved coverage join.

facts.detail: Ofcom published The Communications Market 2026 on 30 June 2026.
The Communications Market Report is provided as an interactive data portal.
The portal includes data collected from industry by Ofcom.
The portal includes data from Ofcom consumer research.
The portal includes headline figures from selected third parties.
Ofcom points to Media Nations for sector commentary and analysis.
Ofcom points to Online Nation for sector commentary and analysis.
Ofcom points to Connected Nations for communications-infrastructure commentary.
Ofcom publishes a short key-findings summary PDF.
The page offers a telecoms-data CSV download.

guard_streams.source: Broadband and landline faults and problems
guard_streams.write_limit: Consumer fault-diagnostic observations and local speed tests do not establish official postcode coverage or parcel-level network availability.

facts.detail: Ofcom lists the faults guide as last updated on 8 April 2026.
Extension leads and wiring changes can introduce interference and lower speed.
Microfilters should be used on each phone socket in relevant setups.
Some electrical devices and wireless emitters can affect routers.
Router position and obstacles can affect wireless range.
Building work and thicker walls can affect broadband speed.
The guide separates equipment or software problems from network faults.
A direct Ethernet connection can help determine whether a line fault exists.
Provider status checkers list known major network problems.
The customer's provider remains responsible for fault resolution and progress updates.
